mainKeyword: best solar panel for pop up camper
guideTitle: Best Solar Panels for Pop-Up Campers (2026)
metaTitle: Best Solar Panels for Pop-Up Campers (2026)
metaDescription: Six solar panels and kits for pop-up campers, built around portable and ground-set panels because a lifting roof cannot carry rigid glass.
expertTake: The Renogy 200W solar blanket is the best fit because it weighs only 8.82 lb, folds small and needs no roof mount. The Newpowa 35W kit is the value pick for a fixed trickle charger on a non-lifting surface. Anyone expecting to run a big fridge or an air conditioner from a pop-up should skip solar and plan for hookups.
introParagraphs: A pop-up camper changes the solar question completely, because the roof is the part that moves. A lifting roof, a fabric tent section and a tight tow weight mean that a rigid glass panel on top is usually the wrong answer, and the places you can bolt something are few.

The practical solution is a portable panel you set on the ground, plus perhaps a small fixed panel on a rigid surface. We evaluated each pick on its spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, comparing weight, folded size, output, connector type and how realistic each one is for a small battery and light loads.

products.name: Renogy 200W N-Type Solar Blanket, 8.82 lb
products.description:
Weight and bulk are the two numbers that matter in a pop-up, and this blanket wins both: 8.82 lb is 54% lighter than a conventional 200W panel, and it folds to about 16 by 15 by 3 inches, small enough for a cabinet or a bin. The listing suggests laying it on the ground, across a vehicle windshield or on a sunny patch, which suits a camper with no roof mount. N-type 16-busbar cells deliver up to 25% efficiency.

A blanket has no frame, so it can be damaged by sharp rocks and it must be weighed down in wind. It is designed for power stations, so check the connector type against your battery or controller and add an MPPT controller if you feed a bare battery. Compared with the SUNIVORA 200W it weighs about seven pounds less and folds far smaller.

Because you handle it daily, treat the folds gently and shake grit from the cells before packing. Keep it dry in storage, and coil the cable loosely. For a pop-up with a small battery and light loads, this is the cleanest solar option.
products.bestFor: Pop-up owners who want a light, compact panel that stores in a cabinet.
pros: Only 8.82 lb, about 54% lighter than a conventional 200W panel
Folds to roughly 16 by 15 by 3 inches
N-type 16BB cells reach up to 25% efficiency
Can lie on the ground or across a windshield
cons: No rigid frame, so it needs weighing down in wind
Designed for power stations, so controller pairing needs checking

products.name: DOKIO 300W N-Type Suitcase Kit With 20A Controller
products.description:
Alligator clips on the leads let you connect this suitcase kit straight to a camper battery, and the included 20A waterproof controller makes it a complete charging system in one case. A 9.8 ft extension cable keeps the controller in shade while the panel sits in the sun, and a 30 degree bracket props it up. The N-type 16-busbar cells sit in an aluminum frame with reinforced corners.

Three hundred watts into a 20A controller at 12V is more than the controller can pass in full sun, since 20A at about 14V is roughly 280W, so you will clip a little on bright days. That is not a problem for a pop-up's small battery, which will be full long before the panel's capacity matters. Unfolded it stretches 78.4 inches, so you need a clear patch of ground.

The case is bulky to store in a pop-up, and it needs a flat spot out of the way of foot traffic. Check the alligator clip teeth for corrosion and consider a ring-terminal lead. It outclasses the Newpowa 35W in charging power but takes much more space.
products.bestFor: Pop-up owners who want a complete plug-and-charge kit and have storage space.
pros: 20A waterproof controller included in the case
300W is the most panel in the lineup with a controller
9.8 ft cable keeps the controller out of the sun
Aluminum frame with reinforced corners
cons: Controller current limit clips the top of 300W at 12V
Large unfolded size and bulky case

products.name: SUNIVORA 200W Portable Panel, 15.9 lb
products.description:
A folding panel with a handle, ETFE surface and IP65 rating, this SUNIVORA is the middle road between the blanket and the suitcase. Its A+ monocrystalline cells convert 22.5% of sunlight, and the 4-in-1 MC4 cable is meant to match several power-station inputs. At 15.9 lb and 24 by 21 inches folded it is easy to carry.

It lacks a controller, so you either feed a power station that has its own MPPT or add a controller for a bare battery. That is simple for a station owner and an extra purchase for a camper-battery owner. Next to the Renogy blanket it is heavier and bulkier but sturdier because of its rigid panels.

The handle makes it easy to move around the site and into the sun. Store it flat, keep the connectors capped, and wipe the surface with a soft cloth. For a pop-up that sees a few weekends a month, it is an accessible choice.
products.bestFor: Pop-up owners with a power station who want a sturdier folding panel.
pros: 22.5% efficiency on A+ monocrystalline cells
Carry handle and 24 by 21 inch folded size
ETFE surface with IP65 rating
4-in-1 MC4 cable fits several stations
cons: No controller, so a bare battery needs a separate one
Heavier and bulkier than the Renogy blanket

products.name: 400W Portable Panel, 36V ETFE, 31.3 lb
products.description:
Four hundred watts on the ground is a lot of power for a pop-up, and this folding panel carries it in a 22.99 by 35.43 by 1.77 inch folded package that weighs 31.3 lb. The ETFE surface, IP67 rating and A+ monocrystalline cells claiming 25% efficiency suit hard outdoor use. A 4-in-1 connector set covers common power-station plugs.

It is also the heaviest and largest panel here, and a pop-up has little spare weight or storage. The 36V class voltage requires a controller or station that accepts it, and it is far more panel than a typical pop-up battery needs. This one fits owners who carry a large power station for a fridge and want to refill it in a day.

Expect to carry it with two hands and to anchor it in wind. Wipe the surface, check the connectors and store it flat. Next to the Renogy blanket it gives double the watts at over three times the weight.
products.bestFor: Pop-up owners with a large power station who want quick refills.
pros: 400W ground output refills a large station quickly
ETFE surface and IP67 rating for rough use
25% efficiency claim on A+ monocrystalline cells
4-in-1 connector set for several stations
cons: 31.3 lb and a large folded size strain a pop-up's weight budget
36V class voltage must match the controller or station input

products.name: Newpowa 35W 12V Panel With Waterproof Controller
products.description:
Small and fixed is the idea: a 35W monocrystalline panel with pre-drilled frame holes, a waterproof controller and 3 ft of pre-attached leads. Its current at maximum power is only 2.04A, so it is a trickle charger that holds a camper battery topped up between trips, not a panel that runs a fridge. The cells are rated at 21 to 23% efficiency.

A pop-up has few places to mount even a small panel, but a fixed, non-lifting surface such as the front storage box or a tongue box may work. At 35W the panel makes roughly 100 to 120Wh on a good day. That is enough to offset self-discharge and a few lights, not to recover from a weekend of use.

It has the lowest cost and the smallest footprint here. Seal the screw holes if you drill into a surface, and check the lead connections. It makes a useful companion to a portable panel, which does the heavy lifting.
products.bestFor: Pop-up owners who want a small fixed panel to keep the battery topped up in storage.
pros: Small fixed panel fits a non-lifting surface
Waterproof controller included in the kit
Pre-drilled frame and pre-attached leads
Keeps the battery topped up between trips
cons: 35W is a maintainer, not a charger for heavy use
Few suitable fixed mounting spots on a pop-up

products.name: SOLPERK 20W Panel Kit With 10A MPPT Controller
products.description:
A glass-faced 20W panel with a 10A MPPT controller and IP67 rating is the lightest answer to keeping a camper battery alive. The A+ monocrystalline cells sit behind low-iron tempered glass in a corrosion-resistant aluminum frame. The controller claims better efficiency than basic units and protects against overcharge.

It is a maintainer, plain and simple. Twenty watts returns around 60 to 80Wh on a good day, which will not recover a battery after a weekend of lights and a pump. For a pop-up that sits in a yard for months between trips, though, it prevents the slow discharge that kills batteries.

It can sit on a dashboard, a tongue box or a stand, and a bracket lets you aim it. Clean the glass, check the clamps and keep the cable tidy. Compared with the Newpowa 35W it offers a better controller but less power.
products.bestFor: Pop-ups that spend months in storage and need a battery maintainer.
pros: Glass-faced panel with an IP67 rating
10A MPPT controller with overcharge protection
Light enough to move or stow easily
Prevents slow battery discharge in storage
cons: 20W cannot recover a battery after heavy use

buyingCriteria.explanation: A lifting roof, a canvas section and tight tow weight mean rigid glass panels on top are usually a poor fit. Check your owner's manual for roof load limits before drilling anything. A portable panel avoids the problem entirely.

The Renogy blanket weighs 8.82 lb and folds to about 16 by 15 inches, while the 400W portable weighs 31.3 lb and folds to 23 by 35 inches. A pop-up has little spare weight or storage, so pick the lightest panel that meets your needs. Weight you tow burns fuel on every trip.

A typical pop-up battery stores only 600 to 1200Wh, so even a 200W panel refills it in a day. A 400W panel is mostly useful for a large power station. Match the panel to your storage, not to the biggest number.

A blanket or foldable panel designed for stations often has MC4 or DC outputs and no controller. If you charge a bare camper battery, add an MPPT controller or choose a kit with one, like the DOKIO 300W with its 20A controller. A wrong pairing can overvolt a controller, and a pop-up battery is usually small enough that a mistake empties or cooks it in a single weekend.

A portable panel needs setting out, aiming and weighing down in wind, and it has to be brought in before a storm. A frameless blanket is easiest to move but easiest to damage. Think about whether you will really handle it every day.

A small fixed panel like the Newpowa 35W or SOLPERK 20W keeps the battery topped up with no effort, while a portable panel does the real charging. Many pop-up owners use both. Decide whether the camper sits stored for long periods, because a camper that sleeps in a driveway all winter needs the maintainer far more than the big panel.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and stowage
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared weight and folded size, since a pop-up has little of either to spare. The Renogy blanket at 8.82 lb and 16 by 15 inches scored highest. The 400W portable at 31.3 lb scored lowest here.

howWeEvaluated.title: Charging usefulness
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared rated watts against a typical pop-up battery. A 200W panel refills a small battery in a day, while 20W and 35W panels maintain. The DOKIO 300W kit's controller made it a complete charger.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controller and connector fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked whether each pick includes a controller and which connectors it ships with. The DOKIO and Newpowa kits include controllers, and the portable panels feed stations. Panels without controllers lost points for bare-battery use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at surface material, IP rating and frame. The glass-faced SOLPERK and the IP67 400W panel scored well, and the frameless blanket scored lower. Hinge and cable strain were noted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: Owner feedback patterns shaped our view of daily handling, wind problems and connector fit. We adjusted for claims that were not tied to a stated figure.

cards.label: Blanket
cards.text: The Renogy blanket is 8.82 lb and folds small. It has no frame, so it needs weighing down and careful handling on rough ground.

cards.label: Suitcase
cards.text: The DOKIO 300W kit is rigid and ships with a controller, but it is bulky to store and long when open.

howToChoose.note: Choose the blanket for weight and storage, the suitcase for a ready-to-use charging kit.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A panel that stores easily, sets up in minutes and refills a small battery by Sunday. Weekend use rarely needs more than 200W.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Renogy 200W blanket fits the weekend case best, with the SUNIVORA 200W as a sturdier alternative.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You camp off-grid for several days. The Renogy 200W blanket or the DOKIO 300W kit give you real recovery.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You camp mostly in campgrounds with hookups. The SOLPERK 20W or Newpowa 35W keep the battery healthy for little.

maintenance.task: Shake out and inspect before folding
maintenance.why: Grit between folds scratches cells and cracks seams. Check the surface before you pack it.
Portable cables flex daily and fail at the connector. Replace any cable with cracked insulation.
A damp panel grows mildew in a storage box. Let it air dry completely.
A maintainer only works if the battery is connected and the panel sees light. Verify the voltage is holding.
Corrosion adds resistance and stops charging. Clean with a wire brush.

faq.q: Can I mount a rigid panel on a pop-up roof?
faq.a: Usually not, because the roof lifts and carries little weight. A portable panel on the ground avoids the problem.

faq.q: How much solar does a pop-up need?
faq.a: For lights, a fan and a pump, 100 to 200W is enough. A fridge or power station may need more.
If you charge a bare battery, yes. Power stations have their own, but a bare battery needs a controller to avoid overcharging.
It is lighter than a framed panel but easier to damage on rough ground. Weigh it down in wind and keep it off sharp rocks.

faq.q: Can I leave a maintainer panel connected?
faq.a: Yes, a good controller stops charging at full and resumes later. Check the battery monthly anyway.
A small 12V fridge can run from a 200W panel and a decent battery. Large three-way fridges need more.
